description: Safety rules for the Linux Command Explainer. See CONTRIBUTING.md → “Adding or changing a safety rule”.

rules.title: Deletes the root or home directory
rules.message: This removes / or your whole home directory recursively. There is no undo and no recycle bin.

safer.why: List exactly what would be deleted before touching it.

rules.title: Deletes a top-level system directory
rules.message: Removing /etc, /usr, /var, /boot, /home, … can leave the machine unbootable or destroy all user data.

safer.why: Inspect the target first.

rules.title: Recursive forced delete (no prompts)
rules.message: `rm -rf` deletes a whole tree without asking and ignores missing files. A typo, an empty variable or a stray space in the path deletes the wrong thing permanently.

safer.why: Same delete, but GNU rm asks once before a recursive removal (-I).
Preview the target before deleting.
Move to the trash instead (trash-cli), so you can recover it.

rules.title: Recursive delete with a glob
rules.message: The shell expands * before rm runs — in the wrong directory it matches the wrong files. `cd dir; rm -r *` is a classic disaster when the cd fails.

safer.why: Prefix with echo to see what the glob expands to.

rules.title: Recursive delete with an unquoted variable
rules.message: If the variable is empty or contains spaces the command targets something else: `rm -rf $DIR/` becomes `rm -rf /`.

safer.why: Quote it and use ${VAR:?} so the command aborts when the variable is empty or unset.

rules.title: Unquoted variable in a destructive command
rules.message: Unquoted variables are split on whitespace and globbed; if empty they vanish and the command runs with other arguments.

safer.why: Quote it ("$VAR") and use ${VAR:?} to abort when unset.

rules.title: Delete target comes from a command substitution
rules.message: The list of files to delete is computed at run time. If the inner command prints nothing unexpected (or fails) the result can differ from what you expect.

safer.why: Print the expanded command first.

rules.title: Moves a top-level system directory
rules.message: Renaming or moving a system directory breaks everything that expects it in place.

rules.title: Moves data into /dev/null
rules.message: Moving files to /dev/null destroys them (and replaces the device node).

rules.title: Silently overwrites existing files
rules.message: cp/mv replace existing destination files without asking.

safer.why: Ask before overwriting (-i), or use -n to never overwrite.

rules.title: find -delete removes every match
rules.message: -delete is immediate and recursive. A wrong path or test deletes far more than intended.

safer.why: Replace -delete with -print to list the matches first.
Keep -delete as the LAST expression — tests after it do not restrict what is deleted.

rules.title: -delete is placed before the tests
rules.message: Expressions run left to right: `find . -delete -name "*.tmp"` deletes EVERYTHING under . because -delete is evaluated first.

safer.why: Put the tests first, -delete last: find . -name "*.tmp" -type f -delete

rules.title: xargs splits on whitespace
rules.message: File names with spaces or newlines are split into several arguments, so the wrong paths get deleted/changed.

safer.why: Use NUL separators (-print0 | xargs -0) or find -exec … +.

rules.title: Parsing ls output
rules.message: ls output is for humans; names with spaces/newlines break. Use find -print0 | xargs -0 or a glob.

rules.title: cd followed by ; and a destructive command
rules.message: With `;` the second command runs even when cd fails — in whatever directory you were in.

safer.why: Use && so it only runs if cd succeeded (or `cd dir || exit 1` in scripts).

rules.title: Irreversibly overwrites data
rules.message: The data is overwritten/discarded and cannot be recovered. On SSDs and journaling/COW filesystems shred is not even a guarantee.

rules.title: Empties a file
rules.message: The file is cut to zero bytes immediately (logs, databases and sockets included).

safer.why: Keep a copy first.

rules.title: Immutable attribute
rules.message: Immutable files cannot be changed or deleted even by root — package upgrades, logrotate and cleanup jobs will start failing.

rules.title: Makes files world-writable
rules.message: Any user or compromised process on the host can modify or replace these files. It is also rarely the actual fix for a “permission denied”.

safer.why: 755 for directories/executables (owner rwx, others r-x); 644 for regular files.
Show the permission of every path component to find the real cause.

rules.title: Recursive permission change on /
rules.message: Changing permissions/ownership of / breaks sudo, ssh, setuid binaries and package management. It usually requires a rescue boot or reinstall.

rules.title: Recursive permission/ownership change on a system directory
rules.message: System directories rely on exact modes/owners (setuid bits, sticky bits, service users). A blanket -R resets them all.

rules.title: Recursive permission/ownership change
rules.message: -R applies the same mode/owner to files AND directories and does not remember the previous values.

safer.why: Save current permissions first (restore with `setfacl --restore=/tmp/perms.backup`).
For modes, treat directories and files separately (use `chmod -R u=rwX,go=rX` for a single capital-X pass).

rules.title: Sets setuid/setgid bits
rules.message: A setuid/setgid binary runs with its owner’s privileges — a classic privilege-escalation path if the file is writable or buggy.

rules.title: Removes all permissions
rules.message: Even you (and services) lose access. On directories this blocks traversal for everything beneath.

rules.title: Very permissive umask
rules.message: New files become world- or group-writable by default.

rules.title: Changes ownership of / or home trees
rules.message: Mass ownership changes can lock users out of their files and break services that rely on their own UID.

rules.title: Recursive ACL change
rules.message: -b removes all ACLs; -R applies recursively. Both are hard to reverse without a backup.

safer.why: Back up ACLs first.

rules.title: dd writes directly to a disk device
rules.message: Everything on the target device is overwritten. Swapping if= and of=, or picking the wrong /dev/sdX, destroys data with no confirmation.

safer.why: Confirm the target device, its size and that it is not mounted.
Add status=progress and conv=fsync; for USB media, unplug other drives first.

rules.title: dd overwrites without asking
rules.message: dd has no confirmation and no dry-run: the output file/device is overwritten from the first byte.

rules.title: Formats a device
rules.message: Creating a filesystem destroys the existing one and (practically) all its data.

safer.why: Check device, filesystem and mountpoint first.
See what is on the device right now.

rules.title: Erases filesystem signatures
rules.message: The device stops being recognised as containing a filesystem/RAID/LVM member, making recovery hard.

safer.why: Dry-run: shows what would be erased without writing.

rules.title: Edits the partition table
rules.message: Partition-table changes can make the data on the disk unreachable. Back up the table first (sfdisk -d).

safer.why: Save the partition table so you can restore it.

rules.title: Repairing a filesystem that may be mounted
rules.message: Never run a repair on a mounted filesystem: it can corrupt data. -y answers “yes” to every fix.

safer.why: Read-only check first (-n makes no changes).
Confirm the device is NOT mounted.

rules.title: Forced / lazy unmount
rules.message: Processes with open files can lose data or hang; lazy unmount detaches while still in use.

safer.why: See what is still using the mount (or `fuser -vm`).

rules.title: Remounts a critical filesystem read-only
rules.message: Services that write logs, sockets or state will fail when / or /var turns read-only.

rules.title: Removes LVM objects
rules.message: Logical volumes / groups disappear with their data. Shrinking (lvreduce) without shrinking the filesystem first destroys data.

safer.why: Review current layout first.
Back up the LVM metadata so it can be restored with vgcfgrestore.

rules.title: Resizes a volume/filesystem
rules.message: Growing is normally safe; shrinking (resize2fs smaller, lvresize -L smaller) can destroy data. Take a snapshot/backup first.

safer.why: Snapshot before resizing.

rules.title: Changes or destroys a RAID array
rules.message: Failing/removing members of a degraded array can cause data loss; --zero-superblock and --create can wipe the RAID metadata.

safer.why: Check array health before touching members.

rules.title: Formats or erases an encrypted volume
rules.message: luksFormat/luksErase destroy the header; without a header backup the data is gone forever.

safer.why: Back up the LUKS header first and store it off the machine.

rules.title: Disables all swap
rules.message: If RAM is nearly full the kernel’s OOM killer starts killing processes. Swapping pages back in can take minutes.

safer.why: Make sure used memory fits into RAM first.

rules.title: Writes to /proc/sysrq-trigger
rules.message: Depending on the key this reboots, powers off or crashes the kernel immediately without syncing disks.

rules.title: Drops the page cache
rules.message: Frees cache but makes the next reads slow; it is not a fix for “high memory use” (cache is reclaimable).

rules.title: Pipes a download straight into a shell
rules.message: You run whatever the server returns — unseen. A compromised host, a changed script or a connection cut mid-download can execute partial or malicious code (often as root).

safer.why: Download, read, then run.
Compare with the checksum/signature published by the vendor.

rules.title: Evaluates remote output
rules.message: Executes downloaded text in your current shell.

rules.title: eval executes arbitrary text
rules.message: If any part of the string comes from a file, variable or user input it becomes command injection.

rules.title: Fork bomb
rules.message: This function copies itself endlessly and exhausts the process table, freezing the machine.

rules.title: Opens a remote shell
rules.message: This pattern gives a remote machine an interactive shell on this host. Only valid in an authorised test.

rules.title: TLS / host verification disabled
rules.message: Anyone on the network path can impersonate the server (man-in-the-middle). Do not do this against production or with credentials.

safer.why: Trust the specific CA instead of disabling verification.
Trust the specific CA instead of disabling verification.

rules.title: SSH host-key checking disabled
rules.message: Disables protection against man-in-the-middle attacks and host impersonation.

safer.why: Pin the key (verify the fingerprint out-of-band) instead of ignoring it.

rules.title: Credentials in a URL
rules.message: User:password in a URL is visible in shell history, `ps`, proxy logs and referrer headers.

safer.why: Use ~/.netrc, an environment variable read from a file, or a credential helper.

rules.title: Secret passed on the command line
rules.message: The value lands in shell history and, while the command runs, in the process list (`ps`) visible to other users.

safer.why: Read it silently instead of typing it into the command.
Start the line with a space (HISTCONTROL=ignorespace), use --password-stdin / env-file / a secrets manager.

rules.title: Password attached to -p
rules.message: The password is visible in `ps` output and shell history.

safer.why: Put credentials in a 600-permission option file, or use plain `-p` to be prompted.

rules.title: docker login with -p
rules.message: The password appears in history and in the process list.

safer.why: Use --password-stdin.

rules.title: Password piped into sudo -S
rules.message: The password sits in plain text in the command line/history.

rules.title: Opens a root shell
rules.message: A permanent root shell has no per-command audit trail and every typo runs as root. Prefer `sudo <command>`.

rules.title: Aggressive port scan
rules.message: Scanning systems you do not own or have written permission to test may be illegal and can trip IDS/IPS or knock over fragile devices.

rules.title: Packet capture may contain secrets
rules.message: Captures can contain passwords, tokens and personal data. Capture the minimum (interface, host, port, -s snaplen), store files securely, delete them afterwards.

safer.why: Limit by packet count (-c) and filter.

rules.title: Attaching strace to a live process
rules.message: Tracing can slow the target 2-50x and, on a busy production process, cause timeouts. Detach as soon as you have what you need.

safer.why: Time-box it and use -c for a summary only (or use perf/bpftrace for low overhead).

rules.title: Attaching gdb to a live process
rules.message: gdb stops the process while attached; quitting without `detach` can kill it. Never leave a debugger attached to a production process.

safer.why: Take a core dump with gcore instead (brief pause only).

rules.title: Kills live TCP connections
rules.message: Matching connections are reset immediately; users and replication links drop.

rules.title: Kills sockets
rules.message: Matching sockets are destroyed immediately.

rules.title: Disables SELinux enforcement
rules.message: Turns SELinux off until reboot. Fix the actual denial instead.

safer.why: Find the denial and fix the label/boolean/policy.
Relabel the files.

rules.title: Permanently disables SELinux
rules.message: Persistent after reboot and removes a whole defence layer.

rules.title: Edits sudoers or account files directly
rules.message: A syntax error in sudoers locks everyone out of sudo; corrupted passwd/shadow can prevent logins.

safer.why: visudo validates the syntax before saving.
Use vipw/vigr for passwd/group edits.

rules.title: Clears shell history
rules.message: Removes the audit trail of what was run — often against policy on shared/production hosts.

rules.title: Kills every process
rules.message: `kill -1` as a PID means “every process you can signal” — as root that is the whole system including sshd.

rules.title: SIGKILL cannot be handled
rules.message: The process gets no chance to flush buffers, release locks or stop children: corrupted data, stale lock/PID files and orphaned workers are common.

safer.why: Send SIGTERM first, wait, and escalate to -9 only if it ignores it.

rules.title: Pattern-based kill
rules.message: The pattern matches by substring: `pkill java` stops every JVM on the host (including other teams’ services).

safer.why: Preview which processes match.
Use -x for an exact name match.

rules.title: Stopping a service you may depend on
rules.message: If you are connected over SSH, stopping ssh or the network can cut you off with no way back except console access.

safer.why: Check what depends on it (`systemctl list-dependencies --reverse {last}`).

rules.title: Restarting sshd with an untested config
rules.message: A syntax error in sshd_config prevents new logins. Existing sessions usually survive — keep one open while testing.

safer.cmd: sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd
safer.why: Validate the config first; open a second session to test before closing the first.

rules.title: Reboots or powers off the machine
rules.message: All services stop; remote sessions are dropped. Confirm the host and that nobody else is using it.

safer.why: See who is logged in and how long the system has been up.
Schedule with a warning (cancel with `shutdown -c`).

rules.title: Reboots or powers off the machine
rules.message: All services stop and remote sessions are dropped. On a remote host you need console/IPMI access if it does not come back.

safer.why: See who is logged in first.
Schedule it with a warning message (cancel with `shutdown -c`).

rules.title: Changes boot behaviour
rules.message: Masking links the unit to /dev/null so nothing (even dependencies) can start it; set-default changes what the machine boots into.

rules.title: Removes the whole crontab
rules.message: -r deletes ALL cron jobs of the user immediately, with no confirmation (it sits right next to -e on the keyboard).

safer.why: -i asks before removing.
Back it up first.

rules.title: Replaces the whole crontab from stdin
rules.message: `… | crontab -` replaces every existing job with the piped text.

safer.why: Append to the existing crontab instead of replacing it.

rules.title: Edits scheduling/logging infrastructure
rules.message: Forces rotation now even if not due — logs may be compressed/removed earlier than expected.

safer.why: Debug/dry-run mode.

rules.title: Changes a kernel parameter at run time
rules.message: Takes effect immediately for the whole host, is lost on reboot unless persisted, and bad values (ip_forward, rp_filter, somaxconn, overcommit) can break traffic or memory handling.

safer.why: Read the current value first and note it for rollback; persist deliberately in /etc/sysctl.d/.

rules.title: Raises a resource limit to unlimited
rules.message: Runaway processes can exhaust memory/descriptors; prefer a sensible number.

rules.title: Reformats swap
rules.message: mkswap wipes the target’s first block.

rules.title: Flushes firewall rules
rules.message: With a default DROP policy you are locked out immediately; with ACCEPT you silently remove protection (NAT/forward rules also vanish — containers and Kubernetes lose connectivity).

safer.why: Back up the rules (nft list ruleset > /root/nft.backup).
Schedule an automatic rollback in case you lock yourself out.

rules.title: Default policy DROP
rules.message: Without an earlier ACCEPT rule for SSH and ESTABLISHED,RELATED traffic, you lose your session instantly.

safer.cmd: iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT && iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
safer.why: Allow established connections and SSH BEFORE changing the policy.

rules.title: Rules are not persistent
rules.message: Rule changes apply instantly but vanish on reboot unless saved (iptables-save / netfilter-persistent / firewalld --permanent).

rules.title: ufw enable / reset
rules.message: Enabling ufw (or resetting it) over SSH can drop your own session if port 22 is not allowed first.

safer.cmd: ufw allow OpenSSH && ufw status verbose
safer.why: Allow SSH before enabling.

rules.title: firewalld panic / removes SSH
rules.message: Panic mode drops ALL packets, including your SSH session.

rules.title: firewalld permanent change
rules.message: Permanent rules apply after --reload or reboot — a mistake can surface later. Test with the runtime config first (omit --permanent), then --runtime-to-permanent.

safer.why: Apply at runtime first; make it permanent once verified (`firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent`).

rules.title: Takes down or flushes a network interface/route
rules.message: If this is the interface or default route you are connected through, the session dies and you cannot bring it back remotely.

safer.why: Run a time-delayed rollback in the background before the risky change.

rules.title: Deletes a user and their home directory
rules.message: The home directory and mail spool are deleted permanently.

safer.why: Keep the home directory, archive it, then delete later.
Archive the home directory first.

rules.title: Replaces all supplementary groups
rules.message: -G without -a REPLACES the user’s group list — e.g. removes sudo/wheel and can lock them out of admin rights.

safer.why: Use -aG to append.

rules.title: Grants a privileged group
rules.message: Membership of sudo/wheel is root; docker/lxd/disk is root-equivalent too. Grant it only deliberately and log why.

rules.title: Removes or locks a password
rules.message: -d makes the account passwordless — anyone can log in locally (and on some PAM setups remotely).

rules.title: Locks an account
rules.message: Locking the only admin or root account can leave nobody able to administer the host.

safer.why: Check another admin exists first.

rules.title: Passwordless sudo
rules.message: Anyone who gets that account (or its SSH key) has unrestricted root.

rules.title: rsync --delete removes files at the destination
rules.message: Anything at the destination that is not in the source is deleted. Swapping source/destination or a missing trailing slash is destructive.

safer.why: Add -n (--dry-run) and add -v to see exactly what would change.

rules.title: Extracts an archive into /
rules.message: Files in the archive overwrite system files with the archive’s owners and modes.

safer.why: List the archive contents first.

rules.title: tar removes source files
rules.message: Originals are deleted after being added. If the archive is corrupt or incomplete they are gone.

safer.why: Verify the archive before deleting the source.

rules.title: Archives with absolute paths
rules.message: Restoring will write to the original absolute locations.

rules.title: sed -i edits files in place
rules.message: The file is rewritten with no undo. A wrong regex corrupts configs; BSD/macOS sed needs `-i ""` and behaves differently.

safer.why: Keep a backup copy (file.bak).
Preview as a diff without changing the file (run the same expression without -i).

rules.title: perl -pi edits files in place
rules.message: In-place edit without a backup if no extension is given (-pi.bak keeps one).

rules.title: xargs feeding a destructive command
rules.message: The argument list comes from standard input — check what is piped in before relying on it.

safer.why: Replace the final command with echo to preview the generated command lines.

rules.title: Overwrites on download
rules.message: Writes a download straight into a system path.

rules.title: Force push rewrites remote history
rules.message: Teammates’ commits on that branch can be erased and their clones diverge. It is the standard way to lose work on shared branches.

safer.why: Fails if someone pushed since you last fetched.

rules.title: Force push to a main/release branch
rules.message: Rewrites history of a shared branch — CI, releases and everyone’s checkouts are affected. Most hosts let you protect these branches.

rules.title: Deletes a remote branch/tag
rules.message: The ref is removed on the remote; others will see it disappear.

rules.title: git reset --hard discards local work
rules.message: Uncommitted changes in tracked files are lost permanently (committed work can be recovered via reflog).

safer.why: Stash (including untracked) first.
Leave a branch pointing at the current commit.

rules.title: git clean deletes untracked files
rules.message: Untracked files are NOT in version control, so they cannot be recovered. With -x it also deletes ignored files such as .env and build outputs.

safer.why: Dry run (-n) lists what would be deleted.

rules.title: Discards all working-tree changes
rules.message: Every unstaged change in the tree is overwritten from the index/HEAD.

safer.why: See what would be lost.
Stash instead of discarding.

rules.title: Force-deletes a branch
rules.message: -D deletes even unmerged branches — commits become unreachable.

safer.why: -d refuses to delete unmerged branches.

rules.title: Rewrites repository history
rules.message: All commit hashes after the change are rewritten; every clone must be re-synced and you need a backup.

safer.why: Take a mirror backup first.

rules.title: Permanently drops unreachable commits
rules.message: Removes the safety net (reflog/unreachable objects) used to recover from mistakes.

rules.title: Skips hooks
rules.message: Bypasses pre-commit/pre-push checks (linting, secret scanning, tests).

rules.title: Prunes Docker objects
rules.message: Stopped containers, unused images/networks and (with volumes) unreferenced data volumes are deleted. Volumes of stopped database containers look “unused”.

safer.why: See what is using space first.
Prune only older objects.

rules.title: Prunes Docker volumes
rules.message: Named volumes not attached to a running container are deleted, including data of stopped databases. This cannot be undone.

safer.why: List candidates and back up what matters.

rules.title: Force-removes containers
rules.message: -f kills running containers; -v removes their anonymous volumes; rmi -f removes images used by containers.

safer.why: Check status and mounts first.
Stop gracefully before removing.

rules.title: Container gets host-level access
rules.message: A privileged container is effectively root on the host; a compromise inside the container becomes a host compromise.

safer.why: Grant only the capability you need (--cap-add=NET_ADMIN) or a specific --device.

rules.title: Mounts the Docker socket or host root
rules.message: Access to docker.sock or / lets the container start privileged containers and read/write the entire host.

rules.title: compose down removes volumes
rules.message: Named volumes (databases, uploads) declared in the compose file are deleted with the stack.

safer.why: Run `down` without -v to keep your data volumes.

rules.title: Image tag is :latest
rules.message: :latest changes under you — pin a version or digest for reproducible deployments.

rules.title: kubectl delete is immediate
rules.message: There is no recycle bin. Controllers recreate pods, but Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs and CRDs stay deleted — and deleting a CRD deletes every custom resource of that kind.

safer.why: Server-side dry run validates and shows what would be deleted.
Export the object(s) first so you can re-apply them.
Confirm the cluster you are pointing at.

rules.title: Deletes all objects of a kind
rules.message: `--all` removes every matching object in scope; combined with -A / --all-namespaces it spans the whole cluster.

safer.why: Dry-run to list the victims.
List what matches first.

rules.title: Deletes a namespace
rules.message: Everything in the namespace is deleted: workloads, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps and PVCs (and the volumes behind them when reclaimPolicy is Delete).

safer.why: Review what lives in the namespace.
Dry run first.

rules.title: Deletes persistent storage
rules.message: Data loss: with reclaimPolicy Delete the cloud disk is destroyed together with the PVC.

safer.why: Check reclaim policies first; patch to Retain if needed.

rules.title: Force delete skips graceful shutdown
rules.message: The object is removed from the API without waiting for the kubelet; a StatefulSet pod can end up running twice (split-brain, volume corruption).

safer.why: Delete gracefully and give it time (`--timeout=120s`).

rules.title: kubectl apply changes the live cluster
rules.message: Applies immediately; whatever differs between the manifest and the live object is changed, including image tags and replica counts.

safer.why: `kubectl diff` shows exactly what would change.
Server-side dry run validates against admission webhooks.

rules.title: apply --prune deletes objects
rules.message: --prune deletes live objects that are not in the applied set (matching the selector).

safer.why: Dry-run and inspect the pruned objects.

rules.title: Delete-and-recreate
rules.message: --force deletes the objects first and then recreates them: downtime and lost status/UID.

rules.title: Scales a workload to zero
rules.message: All pods stop: an immediate outage for that workload.

safer.why: Check autoscalers/PDBs and who depends on it.

rules.title: Evicts all pods from a node
rules.message: Pods are evicted (PDBs may block or, with --disable-eviction/--force, be bypassed). --delete-emptydir-data loses emptyDir contents; unmanaged pods are not rescheduled.

safer.why: Preview which pods would be evicted.
List what runs on the node.

rules.title: NoExecute taint evicts pods immediately
rules.message: All pods without a matching toleration are evicted at once.

rules.title: Restarts every pod of a workload
rules.message: Pods are replaced (rolling). With maxUnavailable/replicas=1, readiness issues or no PDB mean user-visible downtime; `undo` reverts to the previous ReplicaSet — confirm which one.

safer.why: Check the revision history before undoing.
Check disruption budgets.

rules.title: Edits a live object in place
rules.message: Live edits bypass Git/CI, are not reviewed and are overwritten by the next apply (drift).

safer.why: Save the current object for rollback.
Preview the patched object.

rules.title: Prints Secret contents
rules.message: Secret values are only base64-encoded, not encrypted — they land in your terminal scrollback, logs and screen shares.

safer.why: Describe shows keys and sizes without values.

rules.title: Interactive access to a running container
rules.message: Changes made by hand inside a pod are lost on restart and are invisible to your audit trail unless API audit logging is on.

rules.title: Switches the active cluster
rules.message: All following kubectl commands in this shell/session now target the new context — the most common way to run something against production by mistake.

safer.why: Verify before you mutate anything. Consider `--context` per command or kubectx/kubie with a prompt indicator.

rules.title: Grants cluster-admin
rules.message: cluster-admin is unrestricted control of the whole cluster, including secrets.

rules.title: Deletes a CRD
rules.message: Deleting a CRD deletes ALL custom resources of that kind in every namespace.

rules.title: Removes a Helm release
rules.message: Every resource of the release is deleted (hooks may delete data; PVCs of StatefulSets usually remain). History is gone unless --keep-history.

safer.why: Dry run shows what would be removed.
Save values + manifest first.

rules.title: helm upgrade/install changes live resources
rules.message: Chart or values changes roll out immediately; a wrong values file or chart version is applied cluster-wide for that release.

safer.why: The helm-diff plugin shows the exact manifest changes.
Render and validate against the cluster without installing.
Render the manifests locally.

rules.title: helm --force recreates resources
rules.message: --force deletes and recreates resources that cannot be patched — downtime.

rules.title: Secret passed with --set
rules.message: The value ends up in shell history and in the release’s stored values (visible via `helm get values`).

safer.why: Use an existing Secret reference, sealed-secrets/external-secrets, or a values file with 600 permissions.

rules.title: Restores / defragments etcd
rules.message: Restoring replaces cluster state; del removes keys; defrag blocks a member while it runs. A wrong step can take down the control plane.

safer.why: Take a fresh snapshot first.

rules.title: kubeadm reset / upgrade / certs
rules.message: reset removes the node from the cluster and deletes its Kubernetes state; upgrade apply changes the control plane in place.

safer.why: Preview upgrade paths first (and back up /etc/kubernetes + etcd).

rules.title: Applies without showing the plan
rules.message: No review step: any drift, wrong workspace/var-file or typo is applied to real infrastructure immediately.

safer.why: Let Terraform show the plan and ask for confirmation.
Apply exactly the plan you reviewed.

rules.title: Destroys infrastructure
rules.message: Every resource in the state (or the -target set) is deleted — databases, buckets, disks and DNS included unless protected by prevent_destroy.

safer.why: Review what would be destroyed.

safer.cmd: terraform workspace show && terraform state list
safer.why: Confirm the workspace and the resources in scope.

rules.title: Partial apply with -target
rules.message: Skips dependency analysis for everything else; state and config can drift apart. HashiCorp advises it only for exceptional situations.

rules.title: Edits Terraform state by hand
rules.message: State surgery can orphan real resources (they keep existing and costing money) or make Terraform recreate them.

safer.why: Back up the state first.

rules.title: Bypasses the state lock
rules.message: If another run is really in progress, forcing the lock (or disabling locking) can corrupt the state.

rules.title: Forces a resource to be recreated
rules.message: The resource is destroyed and created again: downtime and possible data loss for stateful resources.

rules.title: Secret passed with -var
rules.message: Visible in history and process list.

safer.why: Use TF_VAR_* from a secret store or a -var-file with 600 permissions.

rules.title: terraform apply changes real infrastructure
rules.message: Re-read the plan before typing “yes”: look for lines marked “destroy” or “must be replaced”.

safer.why: Create a saved plan, review it, then `terraform apply tfplan`.

rules.title: Changing module on every host
rules.message: The whole inventory is changed at once, with no canary.

safer.why: Dry-run (`--check --diff`) shows changes without applying them.
Limit to one host first (`--limit <host>`), then a small group.

rules.title: Playbook limited to all hosts
rules.message: Every host in the inventory is changed at once.

safer.why: Dry-run first.
Roll out gradually with --limit <group> and `serial:` in the play.

rules.title: Playbook applies changes
rules.message: Without --check you cannot see what will change first; without --limit it targets every host in the play.

safer.why: Dry-run on a subset first.

rules.title: Ad-hoc shell/command on many hosts
rules.message: Arbitrary commands (or file/package removal) run in parallel on all matched hosts.

safer.why: Test connectivity and scope on one host first.

rules.title: Decrypts secrets to disk
rules.message: `decrypt` writes plaintext secrets to disk (and shell history may keep the vault password).

rules.title: Deletes S3 objects recursively
rules.message: Objects are deleted immediately; on unversioned buckets they are gone for good.

safer.why: --dryrun lists what would be deleted.
Check whether versioning can save you.

rules.title: S3 sync --delete
rules.message: Destination objects missing from the source are deleted. Swapped source/destination arguments wipe the wrong side.

safer.why: Preview first.

rules.title: Deletes a bucket and its contents
rules.message: Bucket and all objects are removed.

rules.title: Makes data public
rules.message: Public buckets are a leading cause of data breaches.

rules.title: Terminates EC2 instances
rules.message: Irreversible: instance-store data and volumes with DeleteOnTermination are lost.

safer.why: EC2 supports --dry-run: checks permissions and parameters without acting.
Confirm the instance identity.

rules.title: Stops EC2 instances
rules.message: Instance-store data is lost on stop, public IPs change unless Elastic IPs are used.

safer.why: Dry-run first.

rules.title: Opens a security group to the internet
rules.message: Ports become reachable from anywhere. Never do this for SSH/RDP/databases.

safer.why: Restrict to your IP/CIDR (--cidr <your-ip>/32) or use SSM Session Manager instead of open SSH.

rules.title: Deletes a database
rules.message: --skip-final-snapshot deletes the DB without a last backup; automated backups are removed with the instance unless retained.

safer.why: Keep a final snapshot.

rules.title: Deletes a managed resource
rules.message: Managed resources are removed — often with no recovery path (KMS key deletion makes encrypted data unreadable after the waiting period; --force-delete-without-recovery skips it).

safer.why: Confirm the account and role you are using.

rules.title: Changes DNS records
rules.message: DNS changes take effect immediately worldwide (cached for the TTL) and can take a service offline.

safer.why: Export the zone first.

rules.title: Grants administrator access
rules.message: Over-broad IAM changes are a common escalation path; access keys are long-lived credentials.

safer.why: Use least-privilege policies, roles with short-lived credentials (SSO/STS) and review with IAM Access Analyzer.

rules.title: Prints secrets
rules.message: Secret values go to your terminal and scrollback; avoid --output text in shared sessions.

rules.title: Deletes a resource group
rules.message: Deletes the resource group and EVERYTHING inside it (VMs, databases, storage, networks); --yes skips the prompt.

safer.why: Keep the confirmation prompt.
Review everything inside first.
Protect important groups with a delete lock.

rules.title: Deletes Azure resources
rules.message: Deletion is immediate; Key Vault purge and storage account deletion are irreversible after retention.

safer.why: Verify names and subscription.
Confirm the active subscription.

rules.title: Deployment in Complete mode
rules.message: Complete mode DELETES every resource in the group that is not in the template.

safer.why: Run what-if to see creates/deletes before deploying.

rules.title: Grants Azure RBAC roles
rules.message: Owner/Contributor at subscription scope is very broad; create-for-rbac prints a secret once.

safer.why: Scope to a resource group and use a built-in least-privilege role or managed identity.

rules.title: Opens a network rule to the internet
rules.message: Ports become reachable from anywhere.

safer.why: Restrict the source to your IP range, or use Bastion/JIT access.

rules.title: Deletes Google Cloud resources
rules.message: Deletion is immediate; deleting a project starts a 30-day shutdown of EVERYTHING in it. --quiet skips prompts.

safer.why: Confirm project/account first.

rules.title: Makes a resource public
rules.message: Grants access to anyone on the internet (or any Google account).

rules.title: DROP / TRUNCATE statement
rules.message: Data or structure is removed immediately and often cannot be rolled back (DDL is auto-committed in MySQL). TRUNCATE ignores row-level safeguards.

safer.why: Take a backup (mysqldump / pg_dump) first.
Run inside a transaction (BEGIN; … ROLLBACK;) on PostgreSQL, and check `current_database()`.

rules.title: DELETE without WHERE
rules.message: Deletes every row in the table.

safer.why: Run the same WHERE as a SELECT first.

rules.title: UPDATE without WHERE
rules.message: Changes every row in the table.

safer.cmd: BEGIN; UPDATE … WHERE …; -- check row count, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK
safer.why: Use a transaction and verify the affected row count.

rules.title: Wipes Redis data
rules.message: All keys (of the DB or the whole instance) are deleted; with replication the wipe propagates to replicas.

safer.why: Take an RDB snapshot first.
Check which DB/instance you are connected to.

rules.title: KEYS blocks the server
rules.message: KEYS scans the entire keyspace in a single blocking call — on a big production instance this stalls every client.

safer.why: SCAN iterates incrementally without blocking.

rules.title: Redis admin command
rules.message: Can stop the server, change replication or reconfigure it live.

rules.title: Drops a database or role
rules.message: The database/role is removed immediately.

safer.why: Dump the target first.
Confirm which server/database you are on.

rules.title: pg_restore --clean drops objects first
rules.message: Existing tables/objects are dropped before they are recreated — on the wrong database that means data loss.

safer.why: Dump the target first.

rules.title: Stops PostgreSQL abruptly
rules.message: Immediate shutdown needs crash recovery; promote makes a standby independent (split-brain risk).

rules.title: VACUUM FULL locks tables
rules.message: Takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and rewrites the table: queries block until it finishes.

rules.title: MongoDB drop
rules.message: Collections/databases are dropped immediately.

rules.title: mysqladmin drop / shutdown
rules.message: Drops databases or stops the server.

rules.title: Removes an essential package
rules.message: Removing core packages can leave the system unbootable or unmanageable (e.g. `yum remove python` removes yum itself).

safer.why: Simulate (-s) to see what else would be removed (dnf: `--assumeno`).

rules.title: Bypasses dependency checks
rules.message: Installs/removes packages ignoring dependencies — the usual way to break the package database.

rules.title: Auto-confirm package changes
rules.message: No chance to read the list of packages that will be removed or upgraded.

safer.why: Read the transaction summary before confirming.

rules.title: Large system upgrade
rules.message: Can replace the kernel, libc, init and many daemons at once — take a snapshot and schedule a reboot window.

safer.why: Review pending upgrades first (dnf: `dnf check-update`).

rules.title: Installs into the system Python
rules.message: Can overwrite packages that the OS tools depend on.

safer.why: Use a virtual environment (or pipx for CLIs).

rules.title: sudo npm install -g
rules.message: Package install scripts run as root.

safer.why: Use a version manager/venv or a per-user prefix instead of sudo.

signals.label: Targets something named “prod”
signals.message: A namespace, context, host, profile, bucket, account or resource-group in this command is named production.
signals.mitigation: Confirm context/account first (`kubectl config current-context`, `aws sts get-caller-identity`, `az account show`, `hostname`), run the read-only or dry-run form, and have a rollback ready.

signals.label: Applies to every namespace
signals.message: The scope is the whole cluster, not one namespace.

signals.label: Applies to all matching objects
signals.message: --all selects everything that matches, not one named object.
signals.mitigation: Name the object or use a label selector (-l app=foo) and list it first with `get`.

signals.label: Force flag bypasses safety checks
signals.message: Confirmations, graceful shutdown or dependency checks are skipped.
signals.mitigation: Remove the force flag and see what the tool refuses — that message is usually the real information.

signals.label: Confirmation prompt skipped
signals.mitigation: Drop the flag so you see the prompt/plan, or run the dry-run variant first.

signals.label: Wildcard in a destructive command
signals.message: A * pattern matches more than you think, and more over time.
signals.mitigation: Print the expansion first: `echo <your glob>` or `ls <your glob>`.

signals.label: Touches a system path
signals.message: System directories and raw devices hold things the OS needs to boot or run.
signals.mitigation: Take a backup/snapshot first (cp -a, etckeeper, LVM/cloud snapshot).

signals.label: Opens access to everyone
signals.message: The target becomes reachable from the whole internet (or any Google account).

signals.label: Security checks disabled
signals.message: TLS or host-key verification is turned off.
signals.mitigation: Trust the specific CA / pin the host key instead.

signals.label: Uses the :latest tag
signals.message: :latest is a moving target — the same command can deploy different code tomorrow.
signals.mitigation: Pin a version tag or digest (image@sha256:…).
